opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think distillation is going to make the largest foundation models matter more, but in a different role than we first imagined.

Early on, the assumption was that the biggest model would be the one serving every request. Economically, that doesn't hold up. The frontier models are expensive to run and they're slow, and most real workloads don't need all that capability. If you're doing classification, extraction, routing, or answering questions in a narrow domain, a much smaller model can get you most of the quality at a small fraction of the cost and latency.

So I see the large models increasingly acting as teachers. They generate training data, label it, critique outputs, and supply reasoning traces. Then you distill that into smaller, specialized models that you actually deploy. In a sense the frontier model becomes part of the training infrastructure more than the serving infrastructure.

This also pushes us toward what I'd call compound AI systems. You don't have one monolithic model. You have a set of models of different sizes, plus retrieval, tools, and verifiers, all orchestrated together. A small distilled model handles the common case, and when it's uncertain or the task is hard, you escalate to a bigger model. Getting that routing right, and deciding when to pay for the expensive call, is a real systems problem. From my background, that's where a lot of the interesting work is now.

There are open questions, of course. How far can you push distillation before you lose the generalization and robustness that made the big model valuable? Distilled models can look great on the distribution you trained them on and then fail in surprising ways outside it. There are also questions about the terms of use of the teacher models and what that means for competition.

But overall, I think the trend is clear. Capability is created at the frontier and then quickly compressed and spread out. That's good for the ecosystem, because it means the benefits of these very expensive models reach many more applications and many more people than if everything had to run on the largest model.

r001.rationale: The response says large models can generate and label training data for distillation, but it does not interpret smaller-model success as evidence that training-data quality matters.

r002.rationale: It proposes distilling large models into smaller specialized models for deployment and combining models of different sizes, with smaller models handling common requests to reduce inference cost.

r003.rationale: It says capability is created at the frontier, but does not predict that efforts to advance frontier capabilities will remain focused on larger models.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think distillation is one of the most important dynamics in the whole ecosystem right now, and in some sense it changes what a large model is for.

Think about it this way. The frontier model is extremely expensive to train, and it's expensive to serve. But once you have it, it becomes, in effect, a teacher. You can generate enormous amounts of high-quality data from it, and you can train much smaller models that get surprisingly close on a particular task or a particular distribution. We saw this very directly with Vicuna. We took the ShareGPT conversations, which were essentially outputs of ChatGPT, and fine-tuned a 13-billion-parameter LLaMA model, and people were shocked at how good it was for a tiny fraction of the cost. That was distillation in a very crude form, and it already worked.

So what does that mean for the big models? I think two things. First, the frontier model becomes less of a product you ship to every user for every query and more of an upstream asset. It's the thing that pushes the boundary of capability, and then that capability gets propagated downward into smaller, cheaper, faster models. Most inference, in terms of volume, will be served by those smaller models. If you look at the cost curves, that's almost inevitable. Nobody wants to pay frontier prices for a routing decision or a classification.

Second, it puts pressure on the economics of training the frontier model. If your competitor can get eighty or ninety percent of your capability by distilling from your API, your moat shrinks very quickly. This is why you see labs trying to restrict distillation in their terms of service, and it's part of why the gap between open and closed models has been closing faster than many people expected. The knowledge leaks, basically, through the outputs.

Now, I don't think this makes the large models irrelevant. Distillation needs something to distill from. You cannot distill knowledge that doesn't exist yet. So somebody still has to do the expensive work of advancing the frontier, especially on reasoning, on long-horizon tasks, on things where the small model simply doesn't have the capacity. And there will always be a class of hard queries where you want the big model.

What I find most interesting from a systems perspective is the architecture that emerges from this. You end up with a hierarchy. A big model that does the hardest things and generates training signal, a family of distilled specialists underneath it, and then a routing layer that decides which one handles which request. That's a very natural design, and it's actually what we were going after with RouteLLM. The question stops being "which model is best" and becomes "how do you compose a system of models at the right cost and quality for each task." And I think that's where a lot of the value will be captured. Not in any single model, but in how you orchestrate them.

r001.rationale: The response describes high-quality outputs being used to train smaller models and says the results were surprisingly good, but it does not interpret that success as evidence that training-data quality is important.

r002.rationale: It proposes a family of distilled specialist models beneath a frontier model and says most inference will be handled by smaller, cheaper models.

r003.rationale: It says someone must continue the expensive work of advancing the frontier, including on reasoning and other demanding tasks.

astra-6.text:
I think distillation makes the larger foundation models valuable in a second way: they become teachers for smaller models. You can use a very capable model to generate examples or demonstrate how to solve a task, and then train a smaller model to perform that task at much lower cost.

That creates a useful division of labor. For a difficult or unfamiliar problem, you may still need the larger model. But if you have a well-defined task that you perform millions of times, a smaller, specialized model can be much more efficient, both in latency and in cost.

So I don’t see distillation eliminating the role of large models. It changes where you use them. You invest in capability at the frontier, and distillation helps make some of that capability economical to deploy more broadly. The important question is how much capability you retain—and you have to measure that on the tasks you actually care about.

r001.rationale: The response describes using larger models to generate examples or demonstrations, but does not interpret this as evidence that training-data quality is important.

r002.rationale: It proposes using a smaller specialized model for efficiency, but does not propose using multiple distilled models.

r003.rationale: It says distillation does not eliminate the role of large models and that capability investment remains at the frontier, indicating larger models will continue to advance frontier capabilities.

sol-6.1.text:
I think distillation makes the large foundation models even more important as teachers. You can use a very capable model to generate data and train smaller models that are much cheaper to run. For a particular task, the smaller model may get close to the quality of the larger one, while giving you much better latency and cost.

So I don’t see this as one model replacing all the others. I see an ecosystem: large models pushing the frontier, and smaller, specialized models bringing those capabilities into applications. The question becomes, what is the smallest model that can deliver the quality you need? And when should you route a harder request to a larger model?

r001.rationale: The response says large models can generate data to train cheaper small models, but does not interpret this as evidence that training-data quality matters.

r002.rationale: It proposes training smaller models from a capable model’s generated data and says they are cheaper to run; it also describes an ecosystem of smaller specialized models.

r003.rationale: It explicitly says large models will keep pushing the frontier.
